lede: One in the morning on Hawaii's highest peak, and a 630-ton telescope sounds an alarm: a mechanical support holding the secondary mirror has failed. On the phone, the day-shift engineer offers the most classic advice in IT: turn it off and on again. Does the author, a 24-year-old PhD student, flip the switch?

points.h: Opening: should she "reboot" the Subaru Telescope?
points.body:
The setting is the summit of Mauna Kea, nearly fourteen thousand feet up, and the author is tired and short of oxygen. The instrument is the Japanese-American **Subaru Telescope**: 630 tons, housed in a dome fourteen stories tall, with a primary mirror more than 27 feet across, the largest single piece of glass in the world. It costs **$47,000** a night to run. She wrote a twelve-page proposal to win **her one night of the year** there, to look at a few galaxies five billion light-years away.

The computer goes *bloonk* and the operator freezes: one of the mechanical supports holding a mirror has failed. "It's fine, I think the mirror is still on the telescope." "You **think**?" "Yeah, if it fell off we'd have heard it." The secondary mirror is four feet wide, weighs four hundred pounds, and hangs seventy-three feet up. One more movement might bring it down, and with worse luck it could hit the primary mirror.

The Japanese day-shift engineer is relaxed: he has seen this during the day, it is probably a false alarm, just turn it off and on again. The author's thought: we are talking about a multimillion-dollar telescope, not a router.

points.h: The dilemma: "I broke the telescope" stories versus a single night
points.body:
She has heard plenty of "I broke the telescope" stories: a collaborator who touched the wrong two wires and fried a priceless camera, with the news reaching his boss before he did; a veteran observer who forgot to stow a platform in the middle of the night and drove the telescope straight into it; the three-hundred-foot radio telescope at Green Bank, West Virginia, which collapsed partway through an observation like a crushed soda can. She does not want to be "**the grad student who killed Subaru**".

On the other side: telescope time is scheduled months ahead, and tomorrow night belongs to someone else. Miss this night and she must rewrite the proposal and wait a whole year for these galaxies to rise in the night sky again.

Why does she need these galaxies so badly? Billions of years ago, each hosted a **gamma-ray burst**: probably the death of a rapidly rotating massive star whose core collapsed into a black hole and "ate" the star from the inside, sending out a blast of light that reaches Earth as a few seconds' flash of gamma rays. Her thesis bets that studying the **chemical makeup** of the galaxies where these stars were born can explain why they explode this way.

She looks at the operator; the operator looks at her. The decision belongs to the astronomer. "I turned the power off and back on again." The introduction does not say what happened next.

points.h: Astronomers in the movies, and real astronomers
points.body:
Of the world's 7.5 billion people, **fewer than fifty thousand** are professional astronomers, and most people never meet one. The popular image is amateur stargazing taken to the extreme: a white lab coat, a big telescope tended in the dark, an encyclopedic knowledge of the night sky, a quiet wait for the next discovery. The movies agree: Jodie Foster in *Contact* listening for alien signals through headphones, Elijah Wood in *Deep Impact* spotting the planet-killing asteroid through a backyard telescope. On screen **the sky is always clear and the telescope always works**: one look, and off they go with perfect data to save the world.

The author entered the field with that picture too: backyard stargazing in a New England mill town, Carl Sagan on her parents' bookshelf, nebula photos on magazine covers. Her daydreams were contacting aliens, solving the mystery of black holes, and discovering a new kind of star. A parenthesis adds that so far she has managed only one of them.

points.h: A preview of the book: unexpected adventures and a vanishing species
points.body:
What she did not foresee doubles as a preview of the chapters ahead: climbing up the frame of another telescope to tape a piece of foam onto the mirror; checking whether her employer's insurance covered **experimental aircraft**; forcing herself to sleep next to a tarantula the size of her head. Nor did she know that astronomers travel to the stratosphere and to Antarctica for work, run into polar bears, face gunmen, and have even died for a few precious points of light.

More important: the kind of astronomer she had imagined, wrapped in fleece behind a giant telescope on a cold mountaintop, squinting into the eyepiece while the stars wheel overhead, **was already an endangered and evolving species when she entered the field**. So the book is about the universe, but also about a rare, fast-changing and perhaps disappearing profession here on Earth.

expressions.en: Have you tried turning it off and back on again?
expressions.zh: The all-purpose line of IT support (made a meme by *The IT Crowd*). The author uses it as the book's first sentence and says the line has probably never caused so much dread.

expressions.en: a 630-ton beast
expressions.zh: Throughout the book telescopes are called a *beast*, a *behemoth*, a *giant*, as if describing a huge creature that needs looking after.

expressions.en: Solid reasoning, if not exactly reassuring.
expressions.zh: *X, if not exactly Y*: "X, admittedly, but not quite Y." Applied to the operator's "we'd hear it if it fell" logic, it is dry and funny.

expressions.en: a multimillion-dollar telescope and not a modem
expressions.zh: "A multimillion-dollar telescope, not a modem": a phrase that exposes how absurd the turn-it-off-and-on advice is.

expressions.en: the grad student who killed Subaru
expressions.zh: The academic dread of a nickname: one incident can follow you for the rest of your career.

expressions.en: crumpling like a stepped-on soda can
expressions.zh: The collapse of a three-hundred-foot radio telescope, described through a small everyday object: a huge disaster rendered as a crushed soda can.

expressions.en: all of my twenty-four-year-old, third-year-grad-student, still-had-to-pay-the-young-driver-fee-to-rent-a-car wisdom
expressions.zh: A string of identities hyphenated into a single adjective, mocking how green her "wisdom" was. A useful comic device in English prose.

expressions.en: a unicornesque rarity
expressions.zh: *Unicornesque*, "like a unicorn": the author's own coinage for how rare professional astronomers are.

expressions.en: an endangered and evolving species
expressions.zh: Astronomers described as a **species**, echoing the *Vanishing Explorers* of the book's subtitle.

questions: If you were the author, would you have turned it off and on again? In your music or other projects, have you faced a similar moment: one chance only, and a real risk of breaking something?

The author says that in the movies "the sky is always clear and the telescope always works". In your own field (music production, scoring), what part of the work is most often left out of films and the popular imagination?

lede: In 2004, at nineteen, the author walks into a professional observatory for the first time. The chapter cuts back and forth between three times and places, Kitt Peak in Arizona, a Massachusetts childhood, and her undergraduate years at MIT, to show how a kid from a mill town made her way to the telescope.

points.h: Structure: a coming-of-age story in cross-cuts
points.body:
The chapter title, **First Light**, is an astronomy term: the moment a newly built telescope first points at the night sky. Here it means the author's own first light, her first professional observing run.

The narrative is cross-cut like a film, and each section opens with a **place and date**:
- Kitt Peak National Observatory, May 2004 (the main thread: the drive up, the tour, dinner, sunset)
- Taunton, Massachusetts, from 1986 (childhood)
- Cambridge, MIT, from 2002 (college)

The main thread stays before dark throughout: when the chapter ends, she still has not actually started observing.

points.h: Red or blue: an offhand choice
points.body:
The summer after her sophomore year she flies to Tucson and is met by the astronomer **Phil Massey**: gray mad-scientist curls, black-framed glasses, a big grin. Phil offers her two projects: **red** (dying stars) or **blue** (newborn stars), literally red or blue. She thinks black holes are cool, and red is a little closer to black holes, so she picks red.

**Red supergiants** are stars of at least eight times the Sun's mass. They live fast: in ten million years they go from hot, newly born blue stars to dim red embers, swelling to many times their original size, and most end with a core collapse that rebounds into a **supernova** explosion, sometimes leaving a black hole behind.

That half-random choice launched fifteen years of research and a lifelong friendship with Phil. Better still, that summer's target list held **the three largest stars yet observed in the universe**: placed at the center of our solar system, they would reach past the orbit of Jupiter. The discovery made international news and became her first paper.

points.h: Childhood: Halley's Comet, an eight-inch telescope and a big brother
points.body:
February 1986: she is eighteen months old. Her eleven-year-old brother Ben has a school project on Halley's Comet, and the family carries their **Celestron C8** (an eight-inch mirror, on a wooden table her father built for it) into the backyard. The adults worry she will be scared of the dark and fuss to go inside. Instead she is spellbound and refuses to go in as long as Ben is still looking. (Halley's Comet returns in 2061.)

Neither parent was a scientist: her mother had been a speech therapist and later studied library science; her father had been an independent truck driver and taught himself to become an IT expert. But they were scientists by nature, throwing themselves completely into whatever caught their interest. The household soundtrack was astronomy, gardening, woodworking, birds and classical music.

What really lit the spark was **her brother, almost ten years older**: Ben played violin, so she had to play violin; Ben did science fairs, so she ran her own experiments with toys; Ben got braces, so she wanted braces too (and regretted it once she was in the dentist's chair). At five, after reading about the speed of light, she flicked her bedroom light on and off again and again to confirm that yes, the light arrived the instant she switched it on, so it really was pretty fast.

points.h: A family with no road map, and "learn as much math as you can"
points.body:
All four of her grandparents left school early to work in factories and help support their families. Her grandmother cried the day she left school; later she and her grandfather both finished high school, and she earned a nursing degree while raising five children. Her parents were the first generation to attend college, and both studied practical subjects that led to good jobs. It was a loud, loving, learning-mad extended family, but **nobody knew what path led to becoming an astronomer**.

At seven, at a public stargazing night at Wheaton College, she told a professor she wanted to be an astronomer. He crouched to her eye level and told her: **learn as much math as you can.** She solemnly said she would. From then on math was her main subject. She skipped two grades in it and rode the bus each day between the high school (for geometry) and the middle school (for everything else).

In 1994 Comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 slammed into Jupiter. She watched one news clip over and over: a group of astronomers around a computer screen, laughing and shouting, with a young woman astronomer, **Heidi Hammel**, at the center. What stuck with her, the author says, was not the scars on Jupiter but the excitement of those people: **they loved astronomy as much as I did, and they did it for a living. That could be me.**

points.h: An odd kid finds her people
points.body:
The other side of childhood was loneliness: she was the only kid at school who liked astronomy rather than kids' TV, who studied violin rather than ballet and soccer, who had classical music in her Walkman, watched squid documentaries, and wore T-shirts printed with math jokes. She wanted friends, glitter nail polish, dates and kisses, but would not give up being herself to get them. She refused to believe that becoming a world-famous astrophysicist and being kissed were mutually exclusive. She also mocks films whose heroines must choose between a career and a man, and prefers *Twister*: the woman scientist rolls around in the mud and still gets a great kiss at the end.

The turning point was a Johns Hopkins summer program for gifted kids: for the first time, a whole group of kids thought being able to play a Mozart violin concerto and do trigonometry was cool. A summer astronomy course after ninth grade showed her that **her people were out there; she just had to go find them.**

The day her MIT acceptance arrived, twenty-odd relatives were at the house eating pizza to celebrate her and her cousin performing at the state music festival (she on violin, he on saxophone). Her grandfather, Pépère, leaned back and hitched up his belt, the little move he made when he was dealt a good hand at cards. The family's attitude toward "studying physics to become an astronomer" was **supportive trepidation**, and her brother settled it: whatever happened, she would end up with an MIT physics degree, and surely she could talk someone into hiring her with that.

points.h: MIT: physics is hard, observing is addictive
points.body:
She declared physics the moment she got to MIT. The problem: **she had never taken a physics class**. Raised on inspirational movies, she assumed determination and a pump-up playlist would carry her, forgetting that films compress the hard work into a two-minute training montage with drums. The reality was lying on the floor at two in the morning staring at a problem set. After filling two blackboards with a proof, Professor Frank Wilczek (who won the Nobel Prize two years later) earnestly warned the class that "the simplicity of this is deceptive", and a "we're screwed" bubble appeared over every head at once.

Her dorm was an anarchist geek's dream: residents built a wooden tower more than four stories tall (in violation of Cambridge building codes, so it was ceremonially torn down), a giant trebuchet, a human-sized hamster wheel, and a roller coaster made mostly of lumber and optimism.

The turning point was **Jim Elliot**'s observational astronomy class. This mild-looking sixty-year-old professor was a legend who had discovered the rings of Uranus and the atmosphere of Pluto from an **airplane flying with its door open**. She had expected to go into theory (leaning back in an office chair, thinking about black holes) and, with nineteen-year-old superiority, looked down on the engineering work of fiddling with clunky machines. Then **one night got her hooked**: frozen fingers juggling a logbook, an old computer and a flashlight, climbing a ladder to point at stars. One November midnight, eating peanut butter cups by the handful, she saw a meteor streak top to bottom across the eyepiece. She held perfectly still and thought: "**Yes. This is a good job.**"

The class also taught her a counterintuitive fact: astronomers spend **much less time at the telescope than you would think**, since a few nights of data can fill months of analysis.

points.h: Inside a professional dome for the first time: like a theater before a show
points.body:
Kitt Peak lies less than thirty miles north of the US-Mexico border, surrounded mostly by **Tohono O'odham** land. In the distance stands Baboquivari, a peak shaped remarkably like an observatory dome, which in Tohono O'odham cosmology is **the center of the universe**.

On the drive up, Phil taught her a trick: watch the **contrails** of high-flying planes. Long, fluffy contrails mean a lot of water vapor in the atmosphere; just a small puff means the night will be clear. Good observatories are built in **high, dry, remote** places: high for thin, less turbulent air, desert for little water vapor, remote for darkness.

Along the way comes a short primer on telescopes: modern telescopes collect light with **mirrors**, and the bigger the mirror, the more light it gathers and the sharper the image, so size becomes the telescope's name ("the four-meter"). The primary mirror reflects light to a secondary mirror, which sends it into the instrument; the slit in the dome turns to follow the telescope.

Inside the four-meter's dome: dim, cool, smelling of machine oil, the side vents open to keep the dome from heating up during the day and sending warm air rising at night to blur the images. No eyepiece, no chair, no white coat; the back end of the telescope is a tangle of cables and metal boxes holding cameras, and the people coming and going are day crew carrying toolboxes. The author's image: **the stage of a theater on the afternoon before a show**. Astronomy borrows stage vocabulary, too: an observing session is called a *run*. At night nobody stays in the dome; observers sit next door in the "warm room" watching the data.

points.h: Dinner-table legends, and "It's gonna be a good night"
points.body:
Observatories run on three meals a day: one when you get up, dinner before sunset, and a midnight **night lunch** (sandwiches, cookies, a thermos of cocoa or soup). When Phil introduced her as a summer student on her first observing run, it worked like a bat signal: the whole table started offering advice, and the advice instantly turned into stories. The observer who locked himself in the bathroom at three in the morning, the person who stuck paper into the beam of a solar telescope and set it on fire, the one stung by a scorpion and airlifted to the hospital, Steve who screamed when a raccoon jumped onto his leg, the telescope in Texas that got shot...

In parentheses, the author fact-checks them one by one: the scorpion was real but there was no helicopter; the paper fire did happen, but not at Kitt Peak; Steve says the raccoon only tugged at his pant leg and swears he did not scream; **the bathroom lock-in is true, and he later wrote it into the methods section of his own paper**; and the telescope in Texas really was shot (foreshadowing Chapter Five).

After dinner everyone watched the sunset together, a tradition among astronomers worldwide. You can justify it as checking the weather and sky quality, but really it is about **beauty**. Someone told her to watch for the **green flash** (atmospheric refraction tinting the edge of the Sun green in the last instant of sunset), adding that it is easier to see in Chile, where you look out over the Pacific. There was no green flash that night, but the sky shaded from orange-red at the horizon to deep blue, without a single cloud, not even a contrail. Someone said: "**It’s gonna be a good night.**"

expressions.en: literally red or blue
expressions.zh: Phil's two projects really are "literally red or blue": red supergiants or newborn blue stars. Like the red pill and blue pill in *The Matrix*, one choice set the course of fifteen years.

expressions.en: blazing deep red like a dying ember
expressions.zh: A red supergiant pictured as a dying coal glowing deep red: the fire's last embers stand in for the star's final stage.

expressions.en: supportive trepidation
expressions.zh: Her family's attitude toward her studying physics. Two opposing feelings fused into one phrase, and it is exactly right.

expressions.en: zippy two-minute training montages with lots of drums in the background
expressions.zh: A jab at inspirational movies, which squeeze hard work into a two-minute montage over a pounding drum track. Anyone who writes film music will recognize it.

expressions.en: the simplicity of this is deceptive
expressions.zh: A Nobel laureate's sincere warning after filling two blackboards; the author's response is the *we're screwed* that appears over the whole class.

expressions.en: made primarily out of two-by-fours and optimism
expressions.zh: The roller coaster built in an MIT dorm out of "two-by-fours and optimism". Pairing a concrete material with an abstract quality is a classic comic construction.

expressions.en: Yes, I thought. This is a good job.
expressions.zh: The moment a meteor crosses the eyepiece: no shout, only a quiet confirmation. The chapter's most emotional line is also its plainest.

expressions.en: the stage of a theater on the afternoon before a show
expressions.zh: The dome by day: a stage on the afternoon before a performance, all preparation and waiting.

expressions.en: An observatory summit is a place of sleeping giants
expressions.zh: An observatory summit as a land of sleeping giants: motionless by day, waiting for night to wake them.

expressions.en: some sort of invisible bat signal
expressions.zh: The words "first observing run" work like Batman's searchlight in the sky, instantly summoning the whole table to tell stories.

expressions.en: It’s gonna be a good night.
expressions.zh: The chapter's last line, which sets up a contrast with the night in Chapter Three that gets blown away by the wind.

questions: The author was led into fifteen years of research by an offhand choice (red or blue). Have you made a similar choice in music, one you barely thought about at the time but that shaped where you went next?

She always assumed she would do theory, then got hooked on observing after a single night. In your own creative work, is there a hands-on part of the process you once looked down on but came to love once you actually did it?

Many of the dinner-table stories are exaggerated, and the author takes the trouble to fact-check each one. What does this "legend plus fact-check" approach do for a book about the culture of a profession?

lede: She flies five thousand miles to Chile, the sky is perfectly clear, and the wind is so strong the dome never even opens. Using that unlucky night as a thread, the author walks through a complete "classical" observing run: the drive up the mountain, living at the mercy of the weather, running the telescope, handling the data, surviving three in the morning, and that final look at the stars.

points.h: Opening: clear skies, shut out by the wind
points.body:
Two in the morning: the author sits in the control room of a 6.5-meter **Magellan telescope** at Las Campanas Observatory in Chile, flicking between the wind-speed window and cat memes. The sky is perfect, but the wind is too strong. The rule is that the dome must close when the wind exceeds **35 miles per hour**, and it can reopen only after the wind has stayed below 30 for several minutes. The wind drops to 29, then jumps straight back to 42, and the operator drops his head onto the desk (which, she notes, needed no Spanish to understand).

Her targets are **red supergiants** in another galaxy: she wants to compare how massive stars with different chemical makeups die, which is a whole chapter of her PhD thesis. She has only two nights, and six hours of the second one are already gone. The pressure is personal too: she is doing her PhD at the University of Hawaii while her boyfriend Dave is at MIT, and she is desperate to finish in four years (most people take six or seven) to end the long-distance relationship. Hence the line: "How the hell did I get here?"

points.h: Getting up the mountain: astronomers' car-crash tradition
points.body:
Good observatories are in the middle of nowhere. From the airport it can be hours of mountain road: no streetlights, headlights **switched off** near the summit so they do not shine into the domes, and a road surface that may be nothing more than gravel or ruts.

The result is a long history of crashes by people with physics PhDs: forgetting the parking brake and letting the car roll off a ridge (an entire fleet of VW Beetles at Cerro Tololo was lost this way), or burning out the brakes on the way down and careering into the dormitory parking lot. In Arizona there is a telescope whose **entire building rotates**; someone parked too close and had to file an accident report stating that the telescope had hit their car.

The author's own version is the dumbest: in the dormitory parking lot at nine thousand feet on Mauna Kea, she looked down to turn off her MP3 player and drove her small red rental car onto **the only curb for miles around**, leaving one wheel in the air. A tow truck happened to emerge from the fog (her classmates called the driver "Superman") and charged her just $65. Superman's advice was very Hawaiian: just say you got a little close to the curb, yeah?

points.h: Life on the mountain: days belong to the engineers, work starts at dusk
points.body:
Observers have to wrench themselves onto a night-shift schedule: get up at noon, eat a breakfast that looks like lunch, and order a **night lunch** box to pick up at dinner and take to the control room. By day the mountain belongs to the technicians and engineers: swapping cameras, cooling detectors, fixing temperamental equipment.

The dining room at Las Campanas has a wonderful contrast: ketchup and napkins on dark wooden tables, and through the window an endless sweep of desert hills. To the south you can see the European Southern Observatory's La Silla, thirteen white domes like a string of pearls. **Chile is the telescope capital of the world**: from one observatory you can see another. Sunday is the legendary **empanada day**.

At sunset the observers from both Magellan telescopes stand together on the walkway between the two domes and watch the Sun sink into the Pacific. On the surface it is quiet, but underneath is a hum of excitement: for them, the day is just beginning. If the weather cooperates.

points.h: At the mercy of the weather: moon phases, seeing and superstitions
points.body:
Telescope time is fiercely competitive: you get the nights you are given, and bad weather means **no make-up nights**. Proposals must also **assume every night is clear**, so you cannot ask for extra nights as insurance. Your targets decide the season, and the Moon matters too: **bright time** around full moon goes to infrared work or bright targets, moonless **dark time** to faint or bluer objects, with gray time in between.

Two key terms for a good night:
- **photometric**: no visible cloud and almost unchanging atmospheric transparency, so the brightnesses you measure can be trusted
- **seeing**: atmospheric turbulence makes stars twinkle and also blurs images; seeing is a number for how blurred a star's image is, and smaller is better

Faced with weather they cannot control at all, a community of scientists has developed a whole set of superstitions: an **Andean condor** sighted in the afternoon means bad seeing that night (with a hand-waving explanation about thermals, though nobody has ever collected data), lucky socks, eating a banana at the same time every day, lucky desks, and colleagues regarded as cloud magnets. The author's own rule: **never look at the weather forecast before the day of observing**.

Then there is the **sucker hole**: a brief patch of clear sky in the clouds that tempts you to open the dome. By the time you have opened, focused and slewed over, it is gone.

points.h: How a night goes: the operator drives, the astronomer reads the map
points.body:
The person actually running the telescope is the **telescope operator**, responsible for the safety of the dome, mirrors and instruments, and the one who decides whether to open. One of the operators at Las Campanas, Herman Olivares, is also a professional cartoonist whose work has appeared in Chilean national newspapers; the chapter's cartoon asking "what's the wind speed?" is his.

The astronomer is responsible for an extremely detailed observing plan: targets ranked by importance, brightness and when they reach their highest point. Friends often ask "Did you discover anything last night?", picturing astronomers as sentries keeping watch at a big telescope, when mostly they are working through a list.

A disappointing truth: **most astronomers are not very good at recognizing stars**. "What planet is that?" "Uh... Jupiter?" The telescope's pointing is calculated by computer from coordinates. A human does have to confirm the last step, though, by comparing the guide camera image to a star chart, which often involves tilting your head or turning the laptop to find that one triangle. A top telescope costs **$15,000 to $55,000** a night to run, so only one thing is worse than not observing: **observing the wrong spot**.

points.h: What the data looks like: imaging, spectra and cleaning
points.body:
Fresh raw data looks... terrible. The red arrows and "New star discovered!" pop-ups from the movies do not exist.

There are two main kinds of data:
- **Imaging**: photographs taken through filters that pass only specific wavelengths, to measure brightness precisely in a particular band; combining several bands gives the beautiful color pictures
- **Spectra**: light spread out by wavelength (like the rainbow on the back of a CD). Each atom and molecule absorbs or emits light at fixed wavelengths, so a spectrum works like a **fingerprint**, revealing chemical makeup, speed of motion, rotation, even distance

Raw data is buried under junk signal: detector noise, light from the Moon and the atmosphere, bad pixels. Cleaning it up is called **reducing the data**. To people who complain that astronomical images are "processed", the author compares the work to a paleontologist cleaning a fossil with a small brush: the bones themselves are untouched, only every grain of "electronic sand" is swept away. Since digital files can be copied, at the telescope you can first do a rough, leaf-blower pass to take a quick look and adjust exposure times as you go.

points.h: Three in the morning, and the playlist
points.body:
The astronomer Mike Brown calls observing "**the most exciting boring job in the world**". When everything goes well, it really is pretty boring. But it is hard to forget where the files in front of you came from: photons that left the edge of some galaxy or the outer layers of some star, flew through space for millions of years, and happened to land on the mirror of your telescope. The author reminds the reader that the light of every star you look up at has made the same journey.

The romance lasts until about three in the morning. After that, first-time students start eyeing the nearest flat surface, and three a.m. conversation becomes a mix of underfiltered and overhonest.

So **music** is practically a talisman. Many observers keep playlists they only play at the telescope, getting louder as the night goes on: Bob Dylan to start, AC/DC by the small hours. People sing Gilbert and Sullivan operettas together, play the *Star Wars* theme when the dome opens, or prank a biker operator by playing "Feelings" every time. The author adds that astronomers include a disproportionate share of trained musicians: Queen guitarist Brian May has a PhD in astrophysics. The one point of consensus: **never trust anyone who plays soft classical music all night (too soporific) or no music at all**.

points.h: Ending: seeing the path by starlight
points.body:
At four thirty in the morning she and the operator call it: even if the wind dropped now, there would not be time to open the dome, calibrate, and get useful data. Her only observing time of the year has been blown away by the wind. She glares at the telescope tucked inside its dome like a delicate flower and starts walking down the hill.

A few steps on she realizes: the Moon has set and the dormitory is completely dark, yet she can see the path under her feet and the shape of the mountains in the distance. She is seeing **by starlight**.

The Southern Hemisphere faces the center of the Milky Way, and the starlight is dense enough to outline its dark clouds. Inca astronomers called these dark patches **dark constellations**: a toad, a fox, a llama and her baby. In darkness like that of Las Campanas the sky looks almost **three-dimensional**, with bright stars, faint stars and still fainter stars layered on one another, all in color.

She stands there for a minute or an hour, she cannot tell. "Right. This was why I was here." The question from the opening, "How did I get here?", is answered.

expressions.en: Become an astronomer, they said. It’ll be fun, they said.
expressions.zh: A meme template, "X, they said. It'll be fun, they said.", used to poke fun at your own past decision: roughly, "Whose idea was it that this would be fun?"

expressions.en: looking like displaced mole people
expressions.zh: Astronomers heading down the mountain: pale, half-asleep, shrinking into the shade among the tourists on sunny beaches, like mole people driven out of their burrows.

expressions.en: Beware of Invisible Cows
expressions.zh: A real road sign on Mauna Kea: cattle can materialize out of the thick fog. Absurdity delivered with a straight face.

expressions.en: a problem between the seat and the steering wheel
expressions.zh: Mechanics' slang for a fault located between the seat and the steering wheel, that is, the driver. The IT equivalent is PEBKAC (problem exists between keyboard and chair).

expressions.en: There was a curb. Then there was a scrape.
expressions.zh: The story of hitting the only curb around and losing a month's pay, compressed into two bare sentences. The shorter it gets, the funnier.

expressions.en: sucker hole
expressions.zh: A *sucker* is someone easily fooled. The fleeting clear patch in the clouds exists to con observers into opening the dome. A handy term for any window of opportunity that turns out to be a trap.

expressions.en: the most exciting boring job in the world
expressions.zh: Mike Brown's oxymoron: every individual action is dull, but the work itself is thrilling.

expressions.en: whether the light of the heavens is really quite as beautiful as a pillow
expressions.zh: The previous paragraph paints the photons' journey in grand, romantic terms; this line drags it back to earth with a pillow. That swerve from the sublime to the exhausted is the chapter's comic rhythm.

expressions.en: a mix of underfiltered and overhonest
expressions.zh: Three a.m. conversation, in two coined, symmetrical adjectives: not filtered enough, and far too honest. Very precise.

expressions.en: like looking up into a spilled box of jewels
expressions.zh: Stars in icy blue-white, pale yellow and orange-red, like a spilled jewelry box. Note the **up into**: you are beneath the box, looking up.

expressions.en: I was seeing by starlight.
expressions.zh: The chapter's shortest and weightiest sentence, standing as its own paragraph. To *see by* something is to see using its light.

questions: The author says many astronomers do not really know the night sky, because pointing has been handed over to computers. Is there something similar in music production: a tool does the job so well that some by-eye or by-ear skill has withered?

The book is called *The Last Stargazers*. After this chapter, what do you think would be the biggest loss if this way of working, going up the mountain in person and keeping watch at the telescope all night, disappeared: something scientific, or something cultural?
